question.prompt: A frog sitting at the point \((1, 2)\) begins a sequence of jumps, where each jump is parallel to one of the coordinate axes and has length \(1,\) and the direction of each jump (up, down, right, or left) is chosen independently at random. The sequence ends when the frog reaches a side of the square with vertices \((0, 0),\) \((0, 4),\) \((4, 4),\) and \((4, 0).\) What is the probability that the sequence of jumps ends on a vertical side of the square?

solutions.title: Use diagonal symmetry
solutions.explanation:
Three possible first jumps land on diagonals of the square. From a diagonal, reflection pairs vertical exits with equally likely horizontal exits.

First, the frog eventually reaches a side with probability \(1\). From any interior lattice point, three consecutive leftward choices force an exit. Each direction has probability \(1/4\), so the chance of exiting within the next three jumps is at least \((1/4)^3=1/64\). The probability of remaining inside after \(k\) blocks of three jumps is therefore at most \((63/64)^k\), which approaches \(0\).

A corner cannot be the first boundary point reached: an axis-parallel jump into a corner would have to start on a side. Thus vertical and horizontal exits are mutually exclusive and together have probability \(1\).

From \((1,1)\) or \((2,2)\), reflect paths across \(y=x\). From \((1,3)\), reflect paths across \(x+y=4\). Each reflection fixes the starting point, preserves the square, and exchanges vertical exits with horizontal exits. It also preserves path probabilities because it merely exchanges the four equally likely jump directions. Hence the vertical-exit probability from each of these three points is \(1/2\).

Now consider the first jump from \((1,2)\). A left jump reaches a vertical side immediately. The other three jumps reach \((1,1)\), \((1,3)\), or \((2,2)\). Combining these four first-jump cases gives
\[
\boxed{\frac14\cdot1+\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac58},
\]
which is choice \(\textbf{B}\).

solutions.title: Set up probability equations
solutions.explanation:
The frog's future depends only on its current position. Assigning an exit probability to each type of interior point lets us average over the four possible next jumps.

Let \(p\) be the probability of eventually exiting on a vertical side from \((1,2)\), \(q\) from \((2,1)\), \(a\) from \((1,1)\), and \(c\) from \((2,2)\). Reflections across \(x=2\) and \(y=2\) preserve vertical exits. Thus \((3,2)\) also has probability \(p\), \((2,3)\) has probability \(q\), and all four points \((1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3)\) have probability \(a\).

A jump onto a vertical side has success probability \(1\); a jump onto a horizontal side has success probability \(0\). Each direction is chosen with probability \(1/4\). Averaging the four neighboring probabilities gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\frac{1+0+p+q}{4},\\
c&=\frac{p+p+q+q}{4}=\frac{p+q}{2},\\
p&=\frac{1+a+a+c}{4},\\
q&=\frac{0+a+a+c}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, from \((1,1)\), left reaches a vertical side, down reaches a horizontal side, up leads to probability \(p\), and right leads to probability \(q\).

Subtracting the last two equations yields
\[
p-q=\frac14.
\]
The first two equations give
\[
2a+c=\frac{1+p+q}{2}+\frac{p+q}{2}
=\frac12+p+q.
\]
Substitute this into the equation for \(q\), then use \(p=q+1/4\):
\[
4q=\frac12+p+q=\frac34+2q.
\]
Therefore \(q=3/8\), and the desired probability is
\[
\boxed{p=\frac38+\frac14=\frac58},
\]
which is choice \(\textbf{B}\).
